result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_semieulerian()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if the graph has an Eulerian path but not an Eulerian circuit. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L19988-L20061){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_semieulerian() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} An Eulerian path is a trail that visits every edge exactly once. A graph is semi-Eulerian if it has an Eulerian path but NOT an Eulerian circuit. For undirected graphs, this occurs when: - the graph is connected - exactly two vertices have odd degree (start and end of path) For directed graphs, this occurs when: - the graph is weakly connected - exactly one vertex has out-degree - in-degree = 1 (start) - exactly one vertex has in-degree - out-degree = 1 (end) - all other vertices have equal in-degree and out-degree ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the graph has an Eulerian path but not circuit, `False` otherwise. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A path graph has exactly two odd-degree nodes (its endpoints), so it's semi-Eulerian: you can trace every edge exactly once, but only if you start and end at those endpoints: ::: {#db471cab .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_path_graph(5) # Returns True (2 odd-degree nodes) graph.is_semieulerian() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: ::: {#1717eed0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Returns False: a path has no closed circuit, only an open trail graph.is_eulerian() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: ::: A cycle graph is the opposite case: it has a full Eulerian circuit, so it's not semi-Eulerian (the two conditions are mutually exclusive): ::: {#229d8ff7 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_cycle_graph(5) # Returns False (has a full Eulerian circuit instead) graph.is_semieulerian() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` False ``` ::: ::: ::: {#795cbc8c .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Returns True graph.is_eulerian() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: ::: The same idea extends to directed graphs, where a directed path has one node with excess out-degree (the source) and one with excess in-degree (the sink): ::: {#9a5af137 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=True) graph.add_path_graph(5) # Returns True (one source, one sink) graph.is_semieulerian() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` True ``` ::: :::
